summaries: Young has a high enough ceiling to finish his career as the most productive option of this class as well as the earliest to make an impact. A Montana/Brees-style field general fused with Wilson/Murray creativity whose floor is lower due to size. If a team leverages his short and intermediate prowess while creating shot plays, he could emerge as a statistical force.

Overall, Young is a size outlier (he will be the smallest quarterback in the NFL the moment he is drafted) with average arm power, but he is a natural passer with an instinctive feel for throw location and play extension. Despite limited physical traits, he has the high-end intangibles and talent required to be an impact starter.

Though stylistically he is like a really impressive karaoke-style version of Patrick Mahomes, he is truly unique as a playmaker.

summaries: Maye is the quintessential Robo-QB: prototypical size, big arm, prolific production, and mobility, but his on-platform accuracy, processing speed, and red-zone game management trail the billing. Needs a spread scheme and patient infrastructure to avoid the Justin Fields trap. Floor is Jake Locker if processing does not improve.

Overall, Maye needs to cut down on the reckless decisions, but he is a well-put-together passer with the on-field command, athletic instincts and arm talent to create solutions for the problems that NFL defenses present. With his physical gifts and smarts, he is cut from the same cloth as Justin Herbert and has a similar ceiling as an NFL player.

Overall, Slovis has the functional skills to be a productive passer when everything around him is going right, but he didn’t put enough on tape to suggest he can elevate an offense when things fall apart around him. He is practice squad candidate who will have a chance to grow into a backup role in the NFL.

Overall, Shipley has only average size, but he runs with controlled athleticism and competitive urgency in all areas of his game. Though he has the mentality of an early-down grinder, his versatile skills fit best in a third-down role and on special teams.

He projects as an NFL complementary back who can be a productive changeup in a committee (like former North Carolina RB Michael Carter).
Fun player; what evaluators imagine when waxing poetic about Bucky Irving.

summaries: Dart pairs solid short and intermediate accuracy with unsettled vertical placement that lacks a clear mechanical fix beyond cleaner climbs and a narrower base. He ideally lands in a West Coast or play-action scheme with moving pockets and a veteran in front of him, or he risks a Jake Locker career outcome. Waiting on NFL draft capital before spending meaningful fantasy resources is the prudent move.

Overall, Dart needs time to develop his progression-based reads and anticipation (things he wasn't asked to regularly do in college), but he is a natural thrower of the football with promising mobility and high-level competitive intangibles. If allowed to develop at his own pace, he offers NFL starting upside in the right situation.

summaries: Ewers sits on the demarcation between potential starter and top-end backup, with polished mechanics, functional pocket feel, and good short-intermediate accuracy that does not carry deep. His brand name and solid drop/release foundation may earn him draft capital above his tape. Best case he is a Desmond Ridder-style early stopgap, more likely a playable journeyman backup.

Overall, Ewers has the arm, intelligence and poise that will translate to the next level, although his up-and-down decision-making, limitations as a play extender and durability concerns create question marks for his pro ceiling. If he stays healthy, the tools are there to compete for NFL starting reps.

Overall, Brosmer is inconsistent when asked to play outside of structure, but he has several redeeming qualities, most notably his intelligence and drive, the chief reasons he can carve out a backup role in the NFL.

summaries: Gabriel has a strong short-range and RPO game with flashes of deep placement, but anticipatory throws against blitzes and black-zone management are persistent holes. Undersized with a three-quarter slot and a tendency to bail rather than climb, he profiles as a compelling backup if the leverage reads and pocket poise mature. Monitor from afar in fantasy until NFL draft capital clarifies the path.

Overall, Gabriel looks small in the pocket and has some limitations as a downfield thrower, but he is a rhythm passer with the football instincts and mature intangibles to overcome his physical shortcomings. A savvy lefty with a quick release, he has similarities to Tua Tagovailoa — and has a fighting chance to earn a backup role in the NFL.

Minor pass-protection and ball-security refinements are all that stand between him and immediate stardom.

Overall, Jeanty displays exceptional contact balance, run instincts and versatility in the passing game, reminiscent of LaDainian Tomlinson. He has the talent to emerge as a high-level running back early in his NFL career.

That’s not a massive red flag — it’s just something to keep in mind.

summaries: Johnson is a plug-and-play wide-zone starter whose one-cut efficiency and forward-lean finishing produce RB2-RB3 value inside his first 2-3 seasons. Passing-down refinement will determine whether he holds three-down duties or gives way to a change-of-pace back.
So while the odds aren’t close to being in his favor, the position itself at least leaves the door cracked open.

Overall, Johnson isn't a dynamic make-you-miss athlete, but he is a patient and powerful one-cut runner with the instinctive vision to crease the defense using run angles and foot quickness. His play style is reminiscent of DeMarco Murray with a three-down skill set to thrive in a zone-based NFL scheme.

Overall, Dekkers' past will be interpreted differently across the league, but the lefty passer has draftable talent and physical and mental tools worth developing.

Overall, Mertz struggled to stay healthy in Gainesville, but he played with improved confidence and better decision-making than what he showed at Wisconsin. He will get his chance to compete for an NFL roster spot, once he's healthy.
Overall, Cook is made of the right stuff, with the functional athleticism and arm to hang in the pros. However, he will need to put more of a premium on ball placement to take the next step.

Overall, Bazelak is physically and mentally tough. He put better consistency on his 2024 tape, from decision-making and execution standpoints, giving himself a chance to play professional football.

Overall, Traore is still young in football years (didn’t play 11-man football until 2020), but he offers intriguing athleticism and pass-catching talent for a developmental F tight end.
